reviewBoundary: Three complete senior mixed practices: five-gap seven-option insertion plus ten-gap form passage each. Fictional class/studio cases and qualified diagram/river/source discussion. Same-author cohesion/variant review, not independent calibration.

units.title: Planning outdoors and using an index
units.alignmentNote: Old sources are level/family drafting references only. Final National I structure: complete five-gap seven-option insertion plus complete ten-gap grammar passage.

materials.title: A. Planning outdoors and using an index
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
An outdoor class event needs more than a hopeful look at the sky. A useful weather plan explains what will happen if the original arrangement cannot go ahead. Thinking about the alternative in advance makes the final decision easier to communicate.

Name the conditions that would change the plan. "Bad weather" may mean different things to different people. ____1____ The conditions should relate to the activity, with safety decisions left to the responsible adults.

Choose a decision time. Families may need to arrange transport, and helpers need to know where to take equipment. ____2____ If conditions change unexpectedly later, send an update rather than pretending the earlier message remains sufficient.

Check the alternative space as carefully as the first one. A room may exist without being large enough or available. ____3____ Moving an event is useful only if the new arrangement can actually work.

Give people one clear place to find the decision. Some may hear a rumour from a friend before reading the official message. ____4____ A consistent source reduces the number of conflicting versions in circulation.

Finally, distinguish cancellation from postponement. ____5____ If there is no new date yet, say so. People can accept uncertainty more easily when they know which part has been decided and which part still needs an answer.
candidates: A. Confirm capacity, access and permission to use it.
B. State whether the event is ending or moving to another date.
C. Explain which weather-related problems matter for this particular event.
D. Ask everyone to rely on the named channel for the current information.
E. Tell them when the initial decision will be announced.
F. Assume every empty-looking room belongs to your group.
G. A plan announced once can never need another message.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: C develops naming activity-specific conditions; the next sentence places safety responsibility. A backup space, B date status, D channel and E decision timing belong elsewhere. F/G ignore permission or change.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 2.
questions.explanation: E gives the announcement time needed for travel/equipment planning. C conditions, A space, D information source and B future date concern different decisions. G denies the later updates explicitly allowed.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A lists the checks needed for an actually usable alternative space. C weather, E timing, D channel and B cancellation status do not establish room suitability. F wrongly assumes ownership.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: D identifies the authoritative current channel, contrasting rumours. A/B/C/E do not resolve inconsistent messages; G forbids updates rather than supplying a current source.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: B defines cancellation versus a move to a different date and prepares the case of no date yet. A/C/D/E concern location, conditions, channel and timing. F/G do not distinguish the two outcomes.

materials.title: B. Planning outdoors and using an index
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
Our teacher asked us to find information in a long book without reading every page. I turned ____1____ (immediate) to the contents page, but it listed only broad chapter headings. The particular tool I wanted did not have a chapter of its own.

A classmate showed me the index ____2____ the back. It listed names and subjects in alphabetical order, together with page numbers. I found several ____3____ (reference) to the tool instead of just one.

The first page explained its basic use. Another contained a photograph, while a third compared an older version with a newer one. The index had helped me find the relevant places, but I still needed ____4____ (read) them to answer the question.

One entry said "see also" and directed me to a related subject. By ____5____ (follow) that link, I discovered a different term for the same kind of tool. Searching only the word I already knew would have missed it.

The book ____6____ (publish) before a recent change to the equipment. Our teacher reminded us ____7____ an index could guide us through a book without making the book current. We noted its date beside our answer.

At the end of the task, I could explain the difference between a chapter list and an index. Neither was ____8____ (good) for every purpose. What mattered was choosing the route ____9____ fitted the question. I wrote the page numbers in ____10____ (I) notebook so that I could return to the evidence instead of relying on memory.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with the correct form of immediate.
questions.explanation: Immediately modifies turned; immediate is adjective and immediacy noun.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: At the back and in the back both locate the index in the rear part of the book. Under/beside the back do not fit this internal location.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with the correct form of reference.
questions.explanation: Several requires plural references. Singular reference and the process form referencing do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with the correct form of read.
questions.explanation: Needed to read is the active infinitive required before them. Bare read and reading do not directly fit this active needed construction.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with the correct form of follow.
questions.explanation: By following uses an -ing clause after by. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with the correct form of publish.
questions.explanation: The singular book receives publication. Simple/past-perfect passive fit; published alone lacks auxiliary and were disagrees.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Reminded us that introduces the statement. What/which cannot introduce this complete declarative clause in the same role; other unlisted readings remain reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with the correct form of good.
questions.explanation: Neither was better for every purpose contrasts the two tools. Best is superlative and more better doubled; unlisted plain adjective readings stay reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 9 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Route is subject antecedent of that/which fitted. Who is human, where not subject and what incompatible with the antecedent.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 10 with the correct form of I.
questions.explanation: My modifies notebook. Personal and independent possessive forms do not directly fit.

units.title: Reading a diagram and tracing a river
units.alignmentNote: Old sources are level/family drafting references only. Final National I structure: complete five-gap seven-option insertion plus complete ten-gap grammar passage.

materials.title: A. Reading a diagram and tracing a river
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
A diagram can make an explanation easier to follow, but it achieves clarity by selecting what to show. Reading one well means noticing its conventions as well as its shapes. The picture and its labels need to be interpreted together.

Begin with the title and the stated purpose. The same object can appear in a diagram of its parts, its movement or its history. ____1____ This prevents you from expecting an answer to a question the drawing was never designed to address.

Read the key before assigning meaning to colours and lines. A red line might represent heat, a route or a boundary. ____2____ Familiar colours do not have one fixed meaning in every subject.

Look for scale information. A tiny feature may be enlarged to make it visible, while distances may be shortened to fit the page. ____3____ A clear arrangement is not necessarily a realistic picture of size.

Follow arrows carefully. They may indicate movement, a sequence or a connection between ideas. ____4____ If the direction matters, reversing it could change the explanation completely.

Finally, connect the diagram back to the accompanying words. ____5____ Where the two seem to disagree, examine labels and assumptions before deciding which is wrong. The value of the diagram lies in the understanding it supports, not simply in how neat it looks.
candidates: A. Check whether the drawing is to scale or deliberately simplified.
B. Decide what kind of relationship the title says it will explain.
C. Treat the key as the guide to those symbols in this particular drawing.
D. The most attractive picture always contains every relevant detail.
E. Ask what each arrow connects and what its direction represents.
F. Each can supply information that the other leaves out.
G. Assume every red line means the same thing everywhere.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B identifies the purpose announced by the title and prepares the warning about irrelevant questions. A scale, C key, E arrows and F text-picture complementarity address other conventions. D/G impose false universals.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 2.
questions.explanation: C ties colour/line meaning to this key, matching the next warning. B purpose, A scale, E arrows and F words are other checks. G directly contradicts the paragraph.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A identifies scale or simplification after examples of enlarged/shortened features. B/C/E/F concern other relationships. D confuses beauty with completeness and G colours with universal meaning.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: E develops arrow movement/sequence/connection and leads to the importance of direction. A/B/C/F do not ask about the endpoints and direction. D/G ignore that relation.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: F refers to diagram and accompanying words, explaining mutual supplementation. A/B/C/E are individual diagram conventions. D claims complete detail and G fixes a colour meaning without evidence.

materials.title: B. Reading a diagram and tracing a river
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
A river does not begin as a wide band of water on a map. Small flows may join together, with water arriving from rain, melting snow or groundwater. The place ____1____ a river is said to begin can depend on the definition used by the mapmaker.

In class, we compared two maps of the same region. One showed only the main river, while the other included many ____2____ (small) streams. The second map was not necessarily describing a different landscape; it was selecting a different level of detail.

Our teacher asked us ____3____ (trace) one route downstream. As tributaries joined, the channel generally carried more water, although the amount also depended ____4____ conditions such as rainfall and water use. A line on a map did not show every change through the year.

We then examined photographs ____5____ (take) at different seasons. Some banks that looked dry in one picture were under water in another. Matching each image to its date was important for understanding the ____6____ (different).

Before ____7____ (draw) a conclusion, we noted what the images could and could not show. They gave us a view of particular places, not a complete measurement of the whole river system.

The activity made ____8____ (we) more careful readers of maps. We learned to look for ____9____ explanation of symbols and scale before comparing two drawings. A simple blue line could represent something ____10____ (constant) changing, and understanding the line meant paying attention to the choices behind it.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Where introduces the place at which the river begins. Which would not supply the needed locative relation and what conflicts with place.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with the correct form of small.
questions.explanation: Smaller/more small compares included tributaries with the main river. Smallest is superlative and more smaller doubled; plain small remains reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with the correct form of trace.
questions.explanation: Asked us takes to trace. Other listed forms do not directly fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Depended on/upon conditions uses that preposition. Other listed prepositions do not complete the pattern.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with the correct form of take.
questions.explanation: Photographs taken is reduced passive for images that were taken. Active taking, base and finite past do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with the correct form of different.
questions.explanation: The difference can be the overall seasonal contrast; differences its several details. Adjective/adverb do not fill the noun slot.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with the correct form of draw.
questions.explanation: Before drawing takes -ing after the preposition. Other listed forms do not fit directly.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with the correct form of we.
questions.explanation: Made takes object us. Subject/possessive forms do not fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 9 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: An explanation uses an before a vowel sound. Other determiner readings remain reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 10 with the correct form of constant.
questions.explanation: Constantly modifies changing. Constant is adjective and constancy noun.

units.title: Comparing accounts and shaping glass
units.alignmentNote: Old sources are level/family drafting references only. Final National I structure: complete five-gap seven-option insertion plus complete ten-gap grammar passage.

materials.title: A. Comparing accounts and shaping glass
materials.instruction: Choose the best sentence for each gap. Two sentences are not needed.
materials.text:
Two accounts of the same event can differ without one being entirely false. Writers select details according to their position, purpose and audience. Comparing accounts is therefore more useful than merely counting how many sentences they share.

Establish what event each account actually covers. One may describe a whole weekend while another focuses on its final meeting. ____1____ A missing detail may lie outside the second writer's chosen period rather than represent a denial.

Separate direct observation from information received later. A writer may have seen one part and learned another from a participant. ____2____ This does not automatically make the account unreliable; it tells you what kind of support each claim requires.

Notice the intended reader. An internal report may explain decisions that a short public notice leaves out. ____3____ More detail does not always mean greater accuracy, but differences of purpose can explain differences of emphasis.

Compare specific claims rather than impressions alone. "They disagree" is less useful than identifying exactly which time, action or explanation differs. ____4____ A precise comparison makes it easier to seek further evidence.

Finally, preserve unresolved differences when the available material cannot settle them. ____5____ A responsible account can state what is supported and what remains uncertain without forcing every source into a single smooth story.
candidates: A. Identify whether a claim was witnessed or reported through someone else.
B. Check whether the apparent gap reflects different boundaries of coverage.
C. Give the conflicting statements clearly enough for someone else to examine.
D. Consider what each audience needed the writer to explain.
E. A writer with the longest account must always be correct.
F. Remove every conflicting claim until the sources appear to agree.
G. Do not turn an unanswered question into a confident conclusion.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B concerns weekend versus final-meeting coverage, preparing the meaning of missing detail. A evidence source, C claim comparison, D audience and G unresolved inquiry serve later gaps. E/F offer unreliable shortcuts.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 2.
questions.explanation: A distinguishes witnessed and reported information and prepares different evidential support. B scope, C claims, D readers and G uncertainty are separate checks. E/F do not identify evidence type.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 3.
questions.explanation: D connects internal/public readership to explanatory purpose. A/B/C/G are other comparisons. E wrongly equates length with truth; F manufactures agreement.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 4.
questions.explanation: C specifies how to state the time/action/explanation conflict for examination. A/B/D/G concern source, scope, audience and unresolved questions. E/F avoid precise comparison.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence for gap 5.
questions.explanation: G preserves uncertainty rather than forcing a smooth final narrative. A/B/C/D are earlier checks, E invents a length rule and F proposes deleting inconvenient conflict.

materials.title: B. Comparing accounts and shaping glass
materials.instruction: Fill each gap with one appropriate word or the correct form of the word in brackets.
materials.text:
At a glass studio demonstration, we watched a maker turn a glowing mass into a small vessel. Visitors stayed behind a marked barrier ____1____ the hot material and tools required controlled working space. The demonstration was not an invitation to try the process ourselves.

The maker worked with an assistant ____2____ prepared equipment and watched the timing. Although one person shaped the main form, the sequence depended on shared ____3____ (attentive). A missed signal could affect the next stage.

As the glass cooled, it became ____4____ (difficult) to shape. The maker returned it to the heat when necessary, explaining that the visible colour was only one part of judging its condition. We were seeing skilled decisions, not simply a fixed recipe acted out by hand.

After ____5____ (form) the vessel, the maker did not place it straight on a cold shelf. It needed a controlled cooling process. The final object would be ready later, so the studio displayed another example from ____6____ previous session.

Our guide invited us ____7____ (compare) the examples rather than assume handmade meant identical. Small differences showed choices in shape and movement, but a visitor could not infer every step from the finished object alone.

I wrote my description ____8____ (careful), distinguishing what I had observed from what the guide had explained. The vessel ____9____ (make) by a trained team under conditions we could only partly understand from a short visit. That did not reduce ____10____ (I) interest. It gave me better questions to ask when I next saw a piece of glass.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 1 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Because/as/since explain the barrier through hot materials and controlled work. Unless makes a condition inconsistent with the described real hazard.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 2 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: Assistant is the defining human subject, who/that. Which is nonhuman, where not subject and whose needs a possessed noun.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 3 with the correct form of attentive.
questions.explanation: Shared attention/attentiveness are nouns for coordinated care. Attentive is adjective and attentively adverb.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 4 with the correct form of difficult.
questions.explanation: The cooling process progressively increases difficulty, more difficult. Difficulter is nonstandard and most difficult is superlative; unlisted plain adjective readings remain reviewable.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 5 with the correct form of form.
questions.explanation: After forming/having formed both describe prior work. Other listed forms do not directly fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 6 with one appropriate word.
questions.explanation: A previous session introduces another session; the previous session can identify the last one. An before consonant p is invalid.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 7 with the correct form of compare.
questions.explanation: Invited us takes to compare. Other listed forms do not directly fit.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 8 with the correct form of careful.
questions.explanation: Carefully modifies wrote. Careful is adjective and carefulness noun.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 9 with the correct form of make.
questions.explanation: Singular vessel receives making: was/had been made. Made alone lacks auxiliary and were disagrees.

questions.prompt: Fill gap 10 with the correct form of I.
questions.explanation: My modifies interest. Personal and independent possessive forms do not modify the noun directly.
